messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amara is a twenty-year-old African woman working as a pharmacist in a busy urban dispensary, currently in a relationship, and presenting with a PCL-5 score of 69. She was referred for psychological assessment after a colleague noticed she had been arriving late to morning shifts and appearing visibly distressed whenever deliveries arrived at the back of the pharmacy — deliveries that sometimes came during rainstorms, when water pooled against the loading dock doors.

The trauma that brought Amara to this point occurred approximately fourteen months ago, when she was detained by a paramilitary group in her country of origin during a period of civil unrest. Over several days, she was subjected to prolonged physical torture in a structure near a flooding river. She was restrained in stress positions for extended periods, her captors issuing commands she was forced to obey under threat of further violence. At one point, the room flooded partially at the ankles. Others detained alongside her did not survive. She was eventually released, and within months had emigrated to the United States to begin her pharmacy training.

What Amara finds most difficult to communicate — to her partner, to her supervisor, to herself — is that the event resists language. She cannot seem to put what happened into words, and the memories that do surface come not as narrative but as sensation: her body suddenly rigid, arms pulled back as though still restrained, breath shallow, the physical posture of captivity returning without warning. She has the distinct impression that whole portions of what happened are missing, that the picture is incomplete, and this incompleteness frightens her as much as what she can recall. These fragmentary, embodied memories are reliably activated by specific sensory encounters. At the pharmacy, when she hears water running through the pipes above the dispensary ceiling during heavy rain, or glimpses flooding on a patient's phone screen, the somatic memories surge before she has time to prepare. Even a raised voice between colleagues — a brief argument over stock inventory — is enough to pull her back. Being asked by her supervisor to cover an unplanned shift, the simple fact of having no choice, can send the same current through her.

Amara has come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that she must remain on guard at all times, because the world has shown her it can become dangerous without warning. This belief — that hypervigilance is not a symptom but a rational necessity — organises much of her daily life. Before she enters any room, including the dispensary storeroom she visits dozens of times each shift, she identifies where the exits are. She sleeps poorly, lying alert in the dark, certain that relaxing her attention would be a mistake. She scans the faces of customers for any resemblance to the men who held her, and on two occasions has left the counter mid-transaction because a man's build or colouring triggered a wave of recognition that felt indistinguishable from real danger. This hypervigilant state keeps her nervous system primed, which means that ordinary triggers — rain on the roof, a colleague's sharp tone — land with the full force of the original event, reactivating the incomplete, wordless memories and confirming to her that the threat is still present. The sense of ongoing threat in turn deepens her certainty that she cannot afford to think about what happened, because she has come to believe she would not be able to handle it if she did — a belief that forecloses the very processing that might bring relief.

Her avoidance has shaped itself around these triggers in ways that have quietly accumulated. She avoids the late shift, when the building is quieter and harder to monitor. She avoids sleep by staying up until exhaustion overtakes her, having learned that certain hours of the evening reliably bring nightmares. She has stopped visiting the break room when a particular male colleague — whose height reminds her of one of her captors — is present. These strategies have reduced her exposure to the worst moments, but they have also kept the memories raw and inaccessible, preventing any coherent account from forming, and sustaining the sense that danger is everywhere and constant. Underneath all of it runs a thread of guilt she rarely speaks aloud: she survived, and others did not, and she has come to feel that her suffering is, in some private way, deserved.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was her partner's distress. He told her gently that he no longer recognised her, that she flinched at kindness, that she seemed to be living somewhere he could not reach. She is most afraid that he is right — and most hoping, though she would not quite say this yet, that some part of what happened can eventually be put into words.
